analysis.one_liner: Adds a voluntary prescription drug benefit to Medicare, covering seniors' medications and pharmacist services.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 26 House members from both parties, never got a hearing or vote; it sat in the House Health Subcommittee until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003, and it died there.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added a new Part D to Medicare: a voluntary program covering outpatient prescription drugs for Medicare beneficiaries. Enrollees would pay a $250 yearly deductible, a monthly premium, and coinsurance capped at 20%. To help pay for it, drug makers would have had to give the program a rebate of at least 18% off their average prices, plus an extra charge when prices rose faster than inflation, with the money used to lower seniors' premiums. Any licensed pharmacy could participate, and claims processors would be barred from setting payment rates or from bulk purchasing. The bill never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who pay out of pocket for prescription drugs would gain a voluntary insurance option covering their medications, including coverage for pharmacist counseling and medication management services. Community pharmacies — including small and rural ones — would gain a new revenue stream, since any willing pharmacy could participate and payment rates had to cover their full costs plus a reasonable return, regardless of their size.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare without drug coverage

how_it_helps.text: It creates a voluntary outpatient prescription drug benefit under Medicare for people entitled to Part A and enrolled in Part B, available beginning January 1, 2003.

Enrollees would pay a $250 annual deductible, a monthly premium set each year by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and coinsurance capped at 20%, with manufacturer rebates deposited in the program's account and used to reduce those premiums.

It also covers medication preparation services (like compounding and special packaging) and medication therapy management services — pharmacist counseling, refill reminders, and monitoring for people taking multiple medications — aimed at preventing adverse drug events and avoiding costlier hospitalizations.

Any licensed pharmacy willing to meet the program's terms could participate, and payment rates may not vary by pharmacy size or prescription volume, with extra incentives for pharmacies in rural and underserved areas.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers would pay mandatory rebates on Medicare-covered drugs; claims-processing intermediaries would be limited to fixed administrative fees and barred from the rebate-negotiation and purchasing roles. Federal taxpayers would appropriate whatever the program cost beyond premiums and rebates, and enrollees would pay the premium, $250 deductible, and up to 20% coinsurance.

drawbacks.text: Enrollees would still owe a $250 annual deductible, a monthly premium set by the Secretary, and coinsurance of up to 20%, so the benefit would not have covered drug costs fully.
The federal government would appropriate whatever amounts were needed beyond premiums and manufacturer rebates to fund the benefit, leaving open-ended the total cost to taxpayers.

The bill bars claims processors from setting payment rates or engaging in aggregate purchasing, and requires pharmacy payment rates to cover all direct and indirect costs plus a reasonable return — provisions that protect small pharmacies but forgo the deeper drug discounts that centralized purchasing might obtain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to seniors is real and large: Medicare in 2002 covered hospital and doctor care but not the outpatient prescription drugs that older patients rely on most, leaving them to pay retail prices at the pharmacy. The main cost concerns are honest ones. A $250 deductible plus coinsurance of up to 20% and a monthly premium would still leave many seniors with meaningful out-of-pocket costs, and the federal government would cover whatever the premiums and manufacturer rebates did not, with no overall spending cap set in the bill. Whether the rebate mechanism — an automatic discount plus a penalty on prices rising faster than inflation — would hold up in practice was untested. The bill's deliberate design choices that favor any willing pharmacy over bulk-purchasing intermediaries protect patients' pharmacy choice and rural access, but they forgo the deeper discounts that centralized purchasing might have won.

outcome.mechanism: The bill never got a hearing or vote — it sat in a House subcommittee from February 2002 until the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and bills that are not passed die when a Congress ends.

narrative.text: Representative Jo Ann Emerson introduced the bill on January 24, 2002, for herself and Representative Mike Ross, to add a voluntary outpatient prescription drug benefit to Medicare.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, then on February 4, 2002 was referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003.
The bill drew 26 cosponsors from both parties: 17 of the 208 House Democrats and 9 of the 223 House Republicans.

The bill would have required drug manufacturers to pay a rebate of at least 18% of the average manufacturer's price plus an inflation-penalty amount on Medicare-covered drugs, with the money used to reduce beneficiary premiums.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers and pharmacy middlemen were better off: the bill died before reaching a vote, so no mandatory manufacturer rebates or restrictions on claims processors took effect.

for.name: Rep. Jo Ann Emerson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare Drug and Service Coverage Act of 2002 on January 24, 2002.

for.name: Rep. Mike Ross
for.what_they_did: Joined Emerson in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral, taking no hearing, markup, or floor action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican led the bill and cosponsorship split 17 Democrats and 9 Republicans, but because no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred, the record shows no partisan divide on the merits.

industries.note: Any maker whose drugs are covered would have to sign an agreement paying a rebate of at least 18% off the average manufacturer's price per unit, plus an extra charge on any price increases above inflation — payments used to hold down seniors' premiums. This directly cut the prices makers could realize on Medicare-covered drugs.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and claims processors
industries.note: The bill would pay contracted carriers only a fixed, competitively bid fee per transaction for processing claims, and expressly bars them from setting payment rates, limiting benefits, choosing pharmacies, or aggregate purchasing — shutting them out of the rebate-negotiation and purchasing role through which PBMs profit.

Any willing licensed pharmacy could join, payment rates had to cover all costs of furnishing the service plus a reasonable return, rates could not vary by pharmacy size or volume, and rural pharmacies would get payment incentives — a structure that favors local pharmacies over large-volume dispensers.
